It might have something to do with stability but I want to make sure that my setup works. I have no camera so I made a simple copy of my rig in 3d as you see below.

![Image](http://web.telia.com/~u13309256/transm_hologram_setup_01.jpg)

The laser is from Integraf and I use it without the lens. The beam spreads pretty wide so thats why I did this setup. The inner beams hits the object on the front and on the left side. The outer beams are weaker and gets reflected by the flat mirror onto the film that is sandwiched between two glass plates. The emulsion side is facing towards the object. The object is not in the way for the reflected beams (I guess it´s important). I have tried different exposure times from 20 sec up to 2 min. Nothing turns up except for some highlights of the ceramic grail on one copy (1 min 30 sec). Do you think my setup would work or should I try something else? But maybe I should try the very simple setup from the Holowiki first.

posts.author: Kaveh
posts.content_md:
First of all, please tell us what software you used to draw the diagram. It's beautiful!

First thing that comes to mind is coherence length. I am not familiar with these new lasers and don't know what coherence length you have. I would ajust the setup to allow for very short coherence length. So the following distances would be equal:

laser - mirror - film

laser - object - film

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Also, sandwiching film is really hard. You may find this article helpful:

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... x_Matching](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/Index_Matching)

Looking at the diagram closley I notice that you have drawn the clamps to be outside the film. The clamps need to cross onto the film in my experience or they bow the glass and allow the center of the film to move.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Yes, the first thing I see is a great difference in path lengths as Kaveh mentioned. Depending on the coherence length of your laser this may be a problem.

The second thing I see is that even though you are not using a beam splitter, that mirror has to be very very stable. Any movement with it and you will lose you holgoram. 

Try a simple single beam hologram first to make sure you film, sandwiching, processing and all other variables are good. Get a good hologram with the Simple SBT and then introduce another mirror for lighting. 

I suggest this set up,

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... ansmission](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/Single_Beam_Transmission)

Then, if you want additional illumination to your object, place mirrors where there is spill over light and redirect that lighting to the object. As you get a hologram you will be able to see if the additional mirror moves as the hologram will be visible but without the additional lighting (from side normally shadowed in a SBT).

posts.author: LarryD
posts.content_md:
> **KungKrille:** Nobody has comments for the setup itself yet except for Kaveh: So you think my setup will work if I adjust the distances? The distance between laser - mirror - film and laser - object is almost equal, so what I need to do is to move the object further away from the film. I hope I can give this a try this weekend.

I have used a similiar setup. In the image it looks like the brightest part of the beam from the laser will be missing both mirror and object. If that is true, i would try to get as much light as possible on the object (rotate laser to the left) and then move your mirror in closer. The goal of this would be to improve the ratio of ref:obj and reduce exposure time a bit.

Also, if the object is dark as shown in your rendering, then try to paint it diffuse white so as to kick back as much light toward the plate.

Once successful, be aware that the diverging beam will make it nearly impossible to do an H2 reflection copy . When you place your film back in the holder in the same orientation to view it, it will look cool, but when you flip it around to project the image for copying, it will be GIANT, and from what I've seen, it continues to scale with distance.

posts.content_md: In your picture you write that the object is stuck in clay. If this is the case maybe the object is moving during the exposure. The object should stand on a hard surface so it won´t move. You can put clay around it to fixate it or even better use hot glue.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
> **KungKrille:** Yes, I read about that setup and I too think it´s wise to try that first . You mentioned using mirrors for wasted light - does it matter if some of it hits the film or should it just be the reference beam and the reflections from the object?

You want to steal light from the reference beam and redirect it to add lighting to just the object. The redirected light should not hit the plate or it will cause noise in the form of a grating being made by the referece beam hitting the plate and the light from the redirecting mirror hitting the plate.

posts.author: ErichRose
posts.content_md: You don't necessarily need laboratory grade equipment. I would start by attaching the mirror to something solid. Many folks have made great use of small weights used for exercise. They can be found and purchased used. You can then either glue the mirror directly or make something adjustable. Others have made great use of small sand-filled containers. The classic is the laser held by a clothes pin stuck in a coffee mug full of sand. All of these methods have one thing in common: weight.
